1870024.fragment: But to think of your mother begging you with her last breath to kneel down and pray for her. And you refused.

range.content: But to think of your mother begging you with her last breath to kneel down and pray for her. And you refused.

1870024.twitter_share_message: “When Mulligan says, “The aunt thinks you killed your mother,” and then charges, “You could have …” —@Genius

children: When Mulligan says, “The aunt thinks you killed your mother,” and then charges, “You could have knelt down, damn it, Kinch, when your dying mother asked you,” he resembles his model
Oliver Gogarty
, who casually declared to all his acquaintances “that Joyce was ‘mad,’ and ‘had killed his mother by telling her what he thought’” (
Ellmann
, 173). But Mulligan overstates the facts, assuming that they were similar to those surrounding Joyce’s mother’s death in August 1903,

Ellmann writes of Mary Joyce’s illness, “Her fear of death put her in mind of her son’s impiety, and on the days following Easter she tried to persuade him to make his confession and take communion. Joyce, however, was inflexible; he feared, as he had Stephen Dedalus say later, ‘the chemical action’ which would be set up in his soul ‘by a false homage to a symbol behind which are massed twenty centuries of authority and veneration.’ His mother wept, and vomited green bile into a basin, but he did not yield. His aunt Josephine Murray argued with him” (129, emphasis added). Four months later, in Mrs. Joyce’s final hours, “she lay in a coma, and the family knelt about her bed, praying and lamenting. Her brother John Murray, observing that neither Stanislaus nor James was kneeling, peremptorily ordered them to do so. Neither obeyed” (136, emphasis added).

Joyce may have refused to compromise his spiritual integrity by making false declarations of faith, but he was not so priggishly self-righteous as to attempt to ruin other people’s spiritual consolations. After his mother’s death, he comforted his nine-year-old sister Mabel, sitting beside her on the stairs with “his arm around her, saying, ‘You must not cry like that because there is no reason to cry. Mother is in heaven. She is far happier now than she has ever been on earth, but if she sees you crying it will spoil her happiness. You must remember that when you feel like crying. You can pray for her if you wish, Mother would like that. But don’t cry any more’” (Ellmann, 136). The Stephen Dedalus of Telemachus was as sensitive to his mother’s suffering as Joyce was to Mabel’s: “Silent with awe and pity I went to her bedside. She was crying in her wretched bed.”

Given such complex family dynamics, the accusation made by Gogarty and Mulligan seems callous and shallow. Joyce felt there was some, but only some, truth to the charge. At the end of August 1904 he wrote to his wife, Nora, “My mother was slowly killed, I think, by my father’s ill-treatment, by years of trouble, and by my cynical frankness of conduct. When I looked on her face as she lay in her coffin—a face grey and wasted with cancer—I understood that I was looking on the face of a victim and I cursed the system which had made her a victim” (Ellmann, 169). But he did not back down from his principled stand about kneeling in prayer. In the following paragraph of the same letter he wrote, “Six years ago I left the Catholic Church, hating it most fervently… . I made secret war upon it when I was a student and declined to accept the positions it offered me… . Now I make open war upon it by what I write and say and do.”

Ulysses appears to heighten and focus the guilt Joyce felt, maximizing its narrative importance as much as the treatment of the black panther episode minimizes the narrative importance of those events. The dream which Stephen had of his mother after death seems to him a kind of malevolent ghostly visitation. His anguish at the ghost’s implicit demand that he kneel down in prayer attains a shattering climax in Circe.

The verbs here play a crucial role in drawing a parallel between his current state of mind and his actions.

He rests his elbow on ‘jagged granite’— something that doesn’t provide comfort but, quite to the contrary, makes him feel more restless, ostensibly from lack of finding anything better suited. Comfort is not Stephen’s priority at the moment.
The ‘fraying’ edge of his coat sleeve could perhaps be an ominous symbol for his own emotional decay: he and his sleeve both are, it could be said, tattered.

The particular quality of the damage to Stephen’s coat is of interest. Frayed edges come from abrasion, as on jagged granite, while shininess comes from pressure, as when resting. Together they give the impression that Stephen’s pose here is a long-held one. As such, they not only communicate Stephen’s poverty but his stasis. As we are shown, Stephen has become ‘stuck’: in his aesthetic pursuits and in Dublin itself.

7792609.twitter_share_message: “Joyce often chooses this slightly unexpected word order in Ulysses. (E.g. “wiped again his razor…” —@Genius

children: Joyce often chooses this slightly unexpected word order in Ulysses. (E.g. “wiped again his razorblade” below.) A more usual syntax would be “lathered his farther cheek again.” The version that stands connects the verb with the idea of repetition before the verb’s object.

One effect of Joyce’s choice is to render the action intrinsically repetitive, rather than incidentally so. That is, the verb becomes “to lather again.” This tells us something about Mulligan’s actions–this is a routine–and perhaps also, if this carries Stephen’s perspective, Stephen’s sense of boredom at watching Mulligan’s show.

Stephen’s point of view certainly seems to be in play throughout this section; his mind concerned with repetition. We have the unhappy replays of his mother’s death, as well as the ‘return’ of his mother in Stephen’s dream.

The syntactical choice also, of course, draws our attention to the broader structure of the novel, which is based on repetition: the text repeats The Odyssey, so that many of the individuals and their actions are versions of something that has happened before. All of these people and their behaviour is intrinsically ‘again’ in Joyce’s system.
Anthony Burgess’s book
Joysprick
spends some time discussing this specific syntactical habit in Joyce’s prose.

More generally, however, this plays with a common metaphor of seeing the writer’s pen as a kind of weapon. Stephen’s interior monologue here recognises that Mulligan’s moments of kindness and conciliation are not necessarily genuine, but in fact indicate an anxiety about his eventual representation in the later writings of Stephen Dedalus. If you take Mulligan as a definite counterpart to
Oliver St John Gogarty

, it seems that this anxiety was warranted. Joyce’s art is concentrated in his “cold steelpen”, an object that suggests the dispassionate recording of what really happened (the coldness, the cold eye) while also being something that could cut and injure as a dagger.

The lancet of Mulligan’s art might well be the surgical instruments he uses as a medical student, which perhaps make Stephen wary. There are doubtless many other suggestions for what Mulligan’s own lancet might be in this case, however.

children: Stephen, like the real James Joyce, had much of his schooling at institutions run by the
Society of Jesus
, a Catholic order better known as the Jesuits: first at the
Clongowes
primary school and then at
Belvedere College
secondary school. Stephen was strongly influenced by his
Jesuit education
which combines rigorous
Aristotelian scholasticism
with strict Catholic zeal, as is depicted in Joyce’s previous novel
A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

. Stephen can’t help thinking in a Jesuit-influenced way even years after he left the church and renounced the Catholic concept of God. Hence Buck claiming that Stephen still has the “jesuit strain” in him, only it goes “the wrong way”: Stephen uses Catholic reasoning to formulate his opposition to Catholicism. Many of his thoughts throughout the book reference thinkers who are key parts of a Jesuit curriculum:
Aristotle
St. Thomas Aquinas
, and Jesuits founder
St. Ignatius of Loyola
(whom Mulligan encourages Stephen to “chuck” a few lines later). Stephen’s anxieties sometimes turn to Catholic conceptions of hellfire and damnation; in chapter 10,
“Wandering Rocks”
, Mulligan suggests this comes from his education by Jesuits who “drove his wits astray [by] visions of hell”, which is why “he can never be a poet”.
